In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken a step closer to Jony Ive's long-held vision of an iPhone that looks like a single piece of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without the Face ID components being visible through the screen, and without compromising display quality in that area, requires some remarkably clever engineering……

Jony Ive once described his long-term design vision for the iPhone as a single sheet of glass; although he has left the company, that goal has remained unchanged. Apple ultimately hopes to embed all the technology that currently takes up screen real estate—including Face ID and the front-facing camera—beneath the display.

The iPhone 18 Pro is the first to achieve this, but the process has been far from simple. Face ID requires the TrueDepth module to both emit and receive infrared light, and infrared cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple had to create gaps between the pixels large enough for infrared light to pass through, without introducing any visible degradation to the display. To achieve this, the company's engineers set about designing an entirely new pixel arrangement that increases the spacing between pixels without affecting display performance.

iFixit demonstrated this pixel arrangement under a microscope, and Apple confirmed to me that overall pixel density across the entire module area is reduced by half. This could have created another problem: halving pixel density might noticeably dim that region of the screen, so Apple compensated by boosting the brightness of those pixels. It also appears to have added an infrared filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further concealing the internal components.

The result is astonishing. In everyday use, even staring very closely, there is absolutely no way to detect the presence of the TrueDepth camera array. Even using macro photography with various screen colours and lighting conditions, I couldn't capture it. That isn't to say it's impossible to detect—as iFixit's microscope footage shows—but in practical use, you will absolutely never notice its presence.

This breakthrough currently allows the Dynamic Island to be reduced in size, enabling it to display three Live Activities instead of two. In some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden beneath the display. This is technically already possible, but the compromises in image quality remain beyond what Apple is willing to accept. Solving this is a matter of when, not if.
